extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, educational psychologists, and mathematics teachers interested in proof and deductive reasoning instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Review and synthesize psychological research on students' ability for deductive reasoning and draw implications for teaching proof across school grades. Emphasizes conceptualization of proof, developmental findings (ages/skills like MP/MT), and two psychological theories with instructional implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of proof (three classroom-centered characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof is a mathematical argument, a connected sequence of assertions for or against a mathematical claim, with the following characteristics: (1) It uses statements accepted by the classroom community (set of accepted statements) that are true and available without further justification; (2) It employs forms of reasoning (modes of argumentation) that are valid and known to, or within, the conceptual reach of, the classroom community; and (3) It is communicated with forms of expression (modes of argument representation) that are appropriate and known to, or within the conceptual reach of, the classroom community. (Stylianides, 2007b, p. 291)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptualization breaks a proof into three components (accepted statements, modes of argumentation, and modes of representation) and stresses balancing 'mathematics as a discipline' (truth, validity, appropriateness in the mathematical community) with 'students as learners' (what is accepted/known/conceptually accessible in the classroom at a given time). Use this definition when evaluating whether a classroom argument qualifies as a proof in that community; consider whether each of the three characteristics is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize proof's domain of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof guarantees the truth of a statement for all the elements in the domain covered by the proof but does not imply anything about the truth of the statement for elements outside that domain (Fischbein, 1982).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or constructing a proof, explicitly identify the domain over which the proof claims to establish truth. Avoid overgeneralization beyond that domain; make domain assumptions explicit in classroom argumentation and in students' written/verbal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the need for a proof (motivating conjectures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful engagement with proof requires the ability to recognize the need for a proof; this need may arise from empirical explorations of mathematical phenomena that lead to the formulation of conjectures that are important to a given classroom community (Balacheff, 1990; Ball & Bass, 2003; Boero et al., 1996).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should create contexts (empirical exploration, puzzling examples, patterns) that generate conjectures valued by the class. Use these as authentic motivations for moving from empirical evidence or examples to general mathematical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the role of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must understand the role of assumptions (e.g., definitions, axioms) that underlie a mathematical argument or a proof (Ball & Bass, 2000; Mariotti & Fischbein, 1997; Stylianides, 2007a; Vinner, 1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to identify and make explicit the assumptions relied on in arguments (definitions, domain restrictions, axioms). Use classroom tasks that require students to vary assumptions and observe effects on conclusions (e.g., showing when a purported proof fails because a hidden assumption was used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple forms of reasoning (inductive, analogical, deductive) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful engagement with proof requires students to use different forms of reasoning (such as inductive reasoning, reasoning by analogy, and deductive reasoning), whose boundaries are often faint. Each form is relevant in different parts of the proving process (e.g., inductive for generalizing from empirical explorations, analogy for generating proof ideas, deductive for constructing or evaluating proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should help students recognize which form of reasoning is appropriate at different stages: use inductive activities to formulate conjectures, analogical tasks to suggest approaches, and explicit deductive work to establish logical necessity. Make transitions between forms explicit in lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive reasoning as logically necessary inference; focus on MP and MT
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive reasoning corresponds to modes of argumentation that are valid and support logically necessary inferences from a given set of premises. Two specific logical rules emphasized are modus ponens (MP): [(p → q) ∧ p] → q, and modus tollens (MT): [(p → q) ∧ ¬q] → ¬p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to recognize and apply MP and MT as central forms of deductive inference. Clarify which proof methods rely on each (MP underlies direct proof and mathematical induction; MT underlies indirect proofs including contradiction and contraposition). Provide worked examples and tasks that isolate these rules and contrast them to non-deductive moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental expectations for deductive reasoning (age/skill trajectory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological research indicates a developmental progression in students' ability for deductive reasoning that extends across the school years; some forms (e.g., MP) appear earlier, whereas others (e.g., MT and full understanding of logical necessity) often emerge later—although empirical findings vary and are sensitive to task content and instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about strict age cutoffs. Expect early emergence of basic deductive moves in elementary grades (especially under supportive instruction), stronger MP competence by late elementary/early adolescence, and more reliable MT competence later unless targeted instruction/training accelerates it. Design curricula that revisit and develop reasoning across grades rather than introducing proofs abruptly only at secondary level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental models theory: stages and instructional implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental models theory (Johnson-Laird) hypothesizes three stages in syllogistic/deductive processing: (1) comprehension—construct a mental model of premises; (2) description—devise a concise description that asserts something not explicit in premises; (3) validation—search for alternative models (counterexamples) to refute the tentative conclusion. Developmental change is driven by improved language competence and increased working memory/processing capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional design should consider working memory limits: reduce the number of alternative models students must hold simultaneously, scaffold model construction, use external representations (diagrams, tokens, written models) to offload memory, and teach explicit strategies for searching counterexamples. Expect one-model problems to be substantially easier than two- or three-model problems; sequence tasks accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic reasoning schema theory: content/context matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatic reasoning schema theory (Cheng & Holyoak) argues that people often reason using domain-specific pragmatic schemas (e.g., permission, obligation) rather than purely formal syntactic rules; performance on conditional reasoning tasks improves when problems map onto familiar pragmatic schemas or everyday contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve students' deductive performance, recast abstract/ formal problems in familiar pragmatic contexts when appropriate, or teach the mapping explicitly between mathematical conditionals and pragmatic schemas. Use familiar, meaningful problem contexts as stepping stones toward abstract formulations, and train transfer from pragmatic to formal settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for psychological theories useful to mathematics educators
rubrics_metrics.description: A psychological theory is especially useful for mathematics educators if: (1) it has significant empirical support; (2) it is widely accepted within psychology (published in high-quality venues and corroborated by independent researchers); and (3) it has been tested with students (not only adults), particularly at schooling levels relevant to mathematics education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting psychological frameworks to inform instruction or curriculum design, prefer theories meeting these characteristics. Use such theories cautiously and look for evidence of applicability to classroom populations and tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional/training effects — classroom conditions matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Research shows that training and supportive classroom environments can improve children's ability for forms of deductive reasoning (e.g., MT) and increase transfer across contexts; mathematics education studies show that, in supportive instruction, even elementary students can construct arguments and proofs using deductive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction that provides targeted training on difficult inference forms (e.g., MT), scaffolds inductive-to-deductive transitions, cultivates classroom norms valuing conjecture and refutation, and leverages tools (dynamic geometry, representations) that support reasoning. Pursue longitudinal/interdisciplinary research to identify how different instructional conditions change developmental trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of argument representation must be appropriate to classroom community
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of argument representation (verbal, pictorial, algebraic, etc.) used to communicate proofs must be appropriate, known to, or within the conceptual reach of the classroom community; different representations can each support valid deductive arguments if they follow from accepted definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow multiple representational forms in classroom proofs, teach translations between representations, and evaluate students' proofs in terms of whether the representation used is appropriate and accessible to that classroom community. Use representational variety as a means to make deductive structure explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working memory and problem-complexity constraints (number of models, syllogistic figure, quantifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Task difficulty in deductive reasoning is determined by factors such as the number of mental models required (one-, two-, three-model problems), the figural arrangement of terms in syllogisms, and complexity of quantifiers; working memory capacity constrains the ability to construct and validate multiple models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence tasks from one-model to multi-model problems; use external supports (diagrams, written notations) to reduce working memory load; provide practice that increases efficiency at maintaining and manipulating temporary models; be aware that time pressure reduces adult performance to levels similar to younger children.
